title: Introduction to Cybersecurity
subtitle: Understand what cybersecurity protects, recognise common threats, and put the essential defences in place on your own accounts, devices and home network.
outcomes: Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability, and use them to judge what's at risk
Recognise common threats such as phishing, malware and ransomware, and the habits that defend against them
Secure your accounts with a password manager, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication
Keep devices updated, and run a backup routine you've proved by restoring a file
Secure a home or small-office network, from the router's settings to the devices on it
Describe the main roles in cybersecurity and plan your next steps into the field
prerequisites: None. You need a computer (Windows, macOS or Linux) and a smartphone that are your own, your own email account, and access to your home router's settings. Every lab is done on your own devices and accounts.
description:
Cybersecurity can sound like a specialist's world, but most of what keeps people and small organisations safe is a handful of well-understood habits, done properly. This course explains the ideas security professionals use every day, confidentiality, integrity and availability, threats, vulnerabilities and risk, and then puts them to work on the things you own.

You'll learn to spot phishing and the tricks behind it, set up a password manager and multi-factor authentication on your most important accounts, keep your devices updated and encrypted, build a backup routine and prove it works by restoring a file and checking its hash, and audit your home network's router, Wi-Fi and firewall. Each module ends with a hands-on lab on your own devices that your instructor reviews, and the course ends with a security plan for a small office. Along the way you'll see the roles that make up the security field, and how to start building experience safely and legally.

modules.title: What cybersecurity protects
modules.summary: The ideas everything else builds on: confidentiality, integrity and availability; threats, vulnerabilities and risk; and the most common attacks and how to defend against them.

lessons.title: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
objectives: Define confidentiality, integrity and availability
Judge which of the three matters most for a piece of information
key_points: Cybersecurity protects information, and the systems that hold it, from being seen, changed or made unavailable by anyone who shouldn't be able to.
Confidentiality means only authorised people can read information; access controls and encryption protect it, and a data leak breaks it.
Integrity means information is accurate and changed only by people allowed to change it; hashes, digital signatures and change records help show nothing has been altered.
Availability means information and systems work when they're needed; backups, spare capacity and quick recovery protect it, while ransomware or an outage breaks it.

These three are often called the CIA triad. Different information needs different protection: for medical records confidentiality may matter most, for a bank balance integrity, and for a shop's website availability.

lessons.title: Threats, vulnerabilities and risk
objectives: Distinguish an asset, a vulnerability, a threat and a risk
Explain defence in depth and least privilege
key_points: An asset is anything of value, a vulnerability is a weakness in it, and a threat is anything that could take advantage of that weakness, from a criminal to a mistake or a flood.
Risk combines how likely something is to happen with how much harm it would do, which helps decide what to deal with first.
Controls reduce risk: preventive controls stop problems (a screen lock), detective controls notice them (a new sign-in alert) and corrective controls recover from them (a backup).
Defence in depth layers controls so one failure isn't enough: a strong password, then multi-factor authentication, then an alert about a new sign-in.
Least privilege means giving each person and program only the access they need, so a mistake or a stolen account can do less harm.

lessons.title: Common threats and how to defend against them
objectives: Recognise the warning signs of phishing and other social engineering
Describe malware and ransomware, and the habits that protect against them
key_points: Phishing messages pretend to come from someone you trust to get you to click a link, open an attachment, share a password or send money; urgency, threats and unusual requests are warning signs.

A web address's hostname runs from after https:// to the next /, and is read from the right: https://login.example.com/ belongs to example.com, but https://example.com.example.net/ belongs to example.net.
When a message asks for something unusual, check it through a channel you already trust, such as a phone number you know or the organisation's own app, never contact details given in the message.
Malware is software made to cause harm, such as stealing data or taking control of a device; it often arrives through phishing, pirated software or programs that haven't been updated.
Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment to unlock them; backups kept offline or with earlier versions let you recover without paying.
Report a suspicious message, and admit a mistaken click quickly: at work tell your IT or security team; at home change the password and check the account's recent activity.

lab.title: Map what you need to protect
lab.goal: Make an inventory of your most important accounts and devices, rate what's at stake using confidentiality, integrity and availability, find out whether your email address appears in known breaches, and practise reading where web addresses really lead.
setup: The starter files security-inventory.md and links.txt

steps.do: Open security-inventory.md. List your five most important accounts (for example email, banking, a phone's cloud account, social media and work or study) and what each holds.

Rate each account High, Medium or Low for confidentiality (if it were exposed), integrity (if someone changed it) and availability (if you lost access to it). Your email account is usually High for all three: it can reset the passwords of most of your other accounts.
List your computer and phone. For each, check that a screen lock is on and that it still receives security updates (Settings shows the version, and whether an update is waiting).
Go to haveibeenpwned.com and check your email address. Note each breach it lists and what was exposed, such as passwords or phone numbers.
steps.see: Either Good news, no pwnage found, or a list of breaches with the data each exposed.

steps.do: For each breach that exposed a password, write down which account you'll change the password on: that account, and any other account that used the same password.
Open links.txt. For each address, find the hostname and read it from the right to decide which site it really belongs to. Write your answers in the Links section, one per line, like 1: example.com.

checks.text: Five accounts and at least two devices are listed, each account rated High, Medium or Low for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
The breach check has been done, with what was found and what will change because of it.
Each address in links.txt is matched to the site it really belongs to; the fifth is a bare IP address with no name, itself a warning sign.

lab.submit: Paste your completed security-inventory.md. Leave out anything you wouldn't want to share, such as account numbers: the ratings and your reasons are what matter.

files.content:

modules.title: Strong authentication
modules.summary: Passwords that hold up, password managers that make them easy, and multi-factor authentication and passkeys, which stop a stolen password from being enough.

lessons.title: Passwords that hold up
objectives: Explain why password length and uniqueness matter most
Choose a strong passphrase
key_points: Passwords stolen in one breach are tried automatically on other sites, so reusing a password lets one breach unlock many accounts; every account needs its own.
Length beats complexity: a passphrase of several random words, or a random password of 15 or more characters, is far harder to guess than a short password with symbols swapped in.
Each word chosen truly at random from a list of 7,776 words, the size of the EFF's diceware list, adds about 12.9 bits of strength, so six random words give about 77 bits.
NIST's digital identity guidelines (SP 800-63B) tell services to check new passwords against lists of breached ones, and not to force regular changes or rules about mixing character types.
Change a password when there's a sign it's been exposed, such as a breach notice, rather than on a schedule; haveibeenpwned.com shows which breaches include your email address.

lessons.title: Password managers
objectives: Explain how a password manager keeps passwords safe
Set up a password manager and protect its vault
key_points: A password manager keeps your passwords in an encrypted vault unlocked by one master password, so every account can have a long, random, unique password you never have to remember.
Password managers fill in a password only on the website it was saved for, which helps protect you from look-alike sites.
Options include managers built into browsers and operating systems, such as Apple Passwords and Google Password Manager, and standalone ones such as Bitwarden, 1Password and KeePassXC.
The master password is the one to make long and memorable, such as a passphrase, and the vault itself should be protected with multi-factor authentication.
Set up recovery before you need it, such as an emergency kit or recovery code stored somewhere safe offline, so losing a device doesn't lock you out of everything.

lessons.title: Multi-factor authentication and passkeys
objectives: Compare the kinds of second factor and how strong each is
Explain why passkeys resist phishing
key_points: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for two or more kinds of proof: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or security key) or something you are (a fingerprint).

A code sent by SMS is better than a password alone but is the weakest second factor, because a phone number can be moved to another SIM by fraud; an authenticator app's codes, which change every 30 seconds, are stronger.
Approve a sign-in prompt on your phone only when you've just tried to sign in yourself: a prompt you didn't expect means someone else has your password, so change it.
Passkeys and hardware security keys (FIDO2 and WebAuthn) are phishing-resistant: they work only on the real site they were created for, so a fake site gets nothing it can use.
When you turn on MFA, save the recovery codes the service gives you somewhere safe and offline, so a lost phone doesn't lock you out.

lab.title: Lock down your most important accounts
lab.goal: Set up a password manager, then secure your email account and one other important account with a unique password, multi-factor authentication and saved recovery codes, and clear out devices and apps that shouldn't have access.
setup: An authenticator app on your phone, or a device that supports passkeys

steps.do: Choose a password manager (one built into your browser or operating system, or a standalone one) and set it up with a long master passphrase.
Turn on multi-factor authentication for the password manager itself, if it offers it, and save its recovery details somewhere safe offline.
In your email account's security settings, change the password to a new one generated by the password manager, at least 16 characters long, and save it in the manager.
Turn on multi-factor authentication for your email account. Choose a passkey, a security key or an authenticator app if the service offers them, rather than SMS. Save the recovery codes offline.
Review the account's signed-in devices and recent activity, and sign out anything you don't recognise. Then review the third-party apps that have access, and remove any you no longer use.
Check the recovery email address and phone number are current: they're how the account gets back to you, or how someone else could take it.
Repeat the password, MFA and review steps for a second important account, such as your bank or main social media account.
Fill in account-checklist.md. Describe what you did and where things are kept, never the passwords or codes themselves.

checks.text: A password manager is in use and its vault is protected by a strong master passphrase.
The email account has a unique generated password and multi-factor authentication, using an app, passkey or security key where the service allows.
Recovery codes are saved somewhere safe offline, and the recovery email and phone are current.
Signed-in devices and connected apps have been reviewed on both accounts.
No passwords, recovery codes or secret keys appear in the submission.

lab.submit: Paste your completed account-checklist.md. Never include a password, recovery code or secret key: describe where they're kept instead.

files.content:

modules.title: Keep devices updated and data recoverable
modules.summary: Updates and patching, the built-in protections every device should have, and backups you've proved you can restore from.

lessons.title: Updates and patching
objectives: Explain why installing updates quickly matters
Find and turn on automatic updates
key_points: Software has flaws, and some are security vulnerabilities; vendors fix them in updates, and publicly known ones get CVE identifiers, such as CVE-2021-44228, so everyone can refer to the same flaw.
Once a fix is published the flaw is widely known, so devices without the update become easier targets; automatic updates close that gap quickly.
Update everything, not just the operating system: browsers, apps, router firmware and smart devices all get security fixes.

Software past its end of support gets no more security fixes: Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025, so a device still running it needs an upgrade, an extended security updates plan or replacing.
A zero-day is a vulnerability that's used before a fix exists; layers such as built-in malware protection, least privilege and backups limit the harm until it's patched.

walkthrough.title: Find the update settings on your devices

steps.do: Windows 11: open Settings | Windows Update. Click Check for updates, and look under Advanced options for the settings that control when updates install.
macOS: open System Settings | General | Software Update. Click the i button beside Automatic updates and turn on the options that install security responses and system files.
Ubuntu: open Software & Updates and its Updates tab, and set When there are security updates to Download and install automatically.
Your browser: open its About page to check for updates. In Chrome or Edge, type chrome://settings/help or edge://settings/help in the address bar; in Firefox, open Help | About Firefox.
steps.see: The version number, and either a message that it's up to date or an update downloading.

lessons.title: Protect your devices
objectives: Describe the built-in protections every device should have turned on
Explain why everyday work should use a standard account
key_points: A screen lock with a PIN, password or biometric stops someone holding your device from using it; set it to lock after a few minutes idle.

Full-disk encryption keeps data unreadable if a device is lost or stolen: BitLocker or Device Encryption on Windows, FileVault on macOS, and LUKS on Linux, which is usually chosen when Linux is installed.
Built-in protection, such as Microsoft Defender Antivirus on Windows and XProtect on macOS, checks for known malware; keep it on and updated.
Install apps only from sources you trust, such as official app stores and developers' own websites, and remove apps you no longer use.
Use a standard (non-administrator) account for everyday work where you can, so software can't make system-wide changes without asking first.
Turn on your device's find-and-erase feature, such as Apple's Find My or its Google and Microsoft equivalents, so a lost device can be located, locked or wiped.

lessons.title: Backups you can restore
objectives: Plan backups with the 3-2-1 rule
Prove a backup works by restoring a file and checking its hash
key_points: A backup is a separate copy of your data that you can restore from; the 3-2-1 rule keeps three copies, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy off-site or in the cloud.
Syncing isn't backing up: a sync service copies deletions and ransomware-encrypted files to every device, unless it also keeps earlier versions you can roll back to.
Keep at least one copy disconnected or versioned, so ransomware or a mistake on your computer can't reach it.
Built-in tools make backups routine: File History on Windows, Time Machine on macOS, and Déjà Dup, shown as Backups, on many Linux desktops.
A backup you've never restored from is a hope, not a plan: test it by restoring a file and checking that it matches the original.
A hash such as SHA-256 is a fingerprint of a file's contents: if a restored file's hash matches the original's, the two files are identical.

steps.do: Windows: open PowerShell in the folder that holds the file (in File Explorer, right-click the folder and choose Open in Terminal) and ask for the file's hash.
steps.see: Algorithm SHA256, then the hash in capital letters, then the file's path.

steps.do: macOS: open Terminal, change to the folder and use shasum with SHA-256.
Linux: open a terminal, change to the folder and use sha256sum.
steps.see: 64 hexadecimal characters, then the file name. Change even one character in the file and the hash changes completely.

lab.title: Set up and test a backup routine
lab.goal: Turn on automatic updates, set up backups with your operating system's own tool, then prove the backup works: delete a test file, restore it and check that its SHA-256 hash is unchanged.
setup: An external drive with free space, or a cloud backup service you use
The starter files backup-test.txt (don't edit it) and backup-routine.md

steps.do: Check for operating system updates, install any that are waiting, and turn on automatic updates (see the lesson walkthrough for where the settings are). Record what you found in backup-routine.md.
Check your browser is up to date from its About page, and record its version.
Put backup-test.txt in your Documents folder and record its SHA-256 hash.
steps.code:
Get-FileHash .\backup-test.txt        # Windows PowerShell
shasum -a 256 backup-test.txt           # macOS
sha256sum backup-test.txt               # Linux

steps.do: Set up a backup of your Documents folder. Windows: Control Panel | System and Security | File History, choose your drive and click Turn on. macOS: System Settings | General | Time Machine, click Add Backup Disk. Ubuntu: open Backups (Déjà Dup), choose the folders and the storage location.
Run the backup now (Run now in File History, Back Up Now in Time Machine's menu, Back Up Now in Déjà Dup) and wait for it to finish.
Delete backup-test.txt from Documents, and empty it from the Recycle Bin or Trash.

Restore it from the backup. Windows: in File History click Restore personal files. macOS: open Documents in Finder and choose Browse Time Machine Backups from the Time Machine menu. Ubuntu: use the Restore tab in Déjà Dup.
Hash the restored file again with the same command and compare.
steps.see: f61fa9a4c66dedbbdb49db13a2dcea6fedf8b526b7b3a5ffcb9e53a61c373292, the same as before (Windows shows it in capital letters, which is the same hash).

steps.do: Finish backup-routine.md: what's backed up, where, how often, which copy is off-site or disconnected, and when you'll next test a restore.

checks.text: The restored test file's SHA-256 hash matches the original exactly.
Automatic operating system updates are on, and the browser is up to date.
A backup routine is written down: what, where, how often, and which copy is off-site or disconnected.
A date is set for the next restore test.

lab.submit: Paste your completed backup-routine.md, including both hash outputs.

files.content:

modules.title: Secure your network, and where to go next
modules.summary: How a home network works and where it's exposed, securing Wi-Fi and connected devices, security basics for a small office, and the roles and first steps of a career in security.

lessons.title: How a home network works, and where it's exposed
objectives: Describe the jobs a home router does
Identify the router settings that matter for security
key_points: A home router usually does several jobs at once: it connects to your internet provider, shares one public address among your devices (NAT), runs the Wi-Fi, hands out local addresses (DHCP) and acts as a basic firewall.
Connections from the internet that your devices didn't start are normally dropped at the router, which is a large part of what protects a home network.
Port forwarding and UPnP open paths from the internet to a device inside; open them only on purpose, and close any you no longer use.
The router's admin page, at a local address such as 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1, controls all this, so its admin password and firmware updates matter as much as any device's.
Remote management lets the router's settings be changed from the internet; unless you need it, keep it turned off.

walkthrough.title: Find your router and check your Wi-Fi's security

steps.do: Windows: find the router's address (the default gateway) and the Wi-Fi security in use.
steps.see: Default Gateway . . . : followed by the router's address, and Authentication such as WPA2-Personal or WPA3-Personal.

steps.do: macOS: find the default gateway; then hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon in the menu bar to see the Security of your network.
steps.see: gateway: followed by the router's address.

steps.do: Linux: find the default route, and the security of the Wi-Fi network you're on (marked with yes in the ACTIVE column).
steps.code:
ip route show default
nmcli -f ACTIVE,SSID,SECURITY dev wifi
steps.see: default via followed by the router's address, and WPA2 or WPA3 for your network.

steps.do: Type the router's address into a browser to open its admin page, and sign in with the admin password, often printed on a label on the router if it's never been changed.

lessons.title: Securing Wi-Fi and connected devices
objectives: Choose secure Wi-Fi settings
Keep smart devices from putting the rest of the network at risk
key_points: Use WPA3, or WPA2 with AES where some devices can't use WPA3; WEP and WPA with TKIP are broken and shouldn't be used.
A long, unique Wi-Fi passphrase matters because anyone in range can try to guess it; change it if it has been shared widely.
Turn off WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup), or at least its PIN method, if your router allows: the PIN's design lets it be guessed far faster than its length suggests.
Put visitors and smart devices, such as cameras, TVs and speakers, on a guest network, so a weak device can't reach your computers.
Change every device's default password, keep its firmware updated and turn off features you don't use; a device that no longer gets updates should be replaced, or at least kept on the guest network.

lessons.title: Security basics for a small office
objectives: Apply home-network habits to a small office
Name the basic controls a small organisation needs
key_points: Keep an inventory of the office's devices, accounts and data, with who's responsible for each: you can't protect what you don't know you have.
Give everyone their own account, never shared logins, with administrator rights only for those who need them, and remove access on the day someone leaves.
Separate networks where the equipment allows: staff devices on one, guests and smart devices on another, and card terminals or servers on their own.
Schemes such as the UK's Cyber Essentials build on five basic controls: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and security update management.
Write a one-page plan for when something goes wrong: who to call, how to disconnect an affected device, where the backups are and how to restore them.

lessons.title: Careers in cybersecurity
objectives: Describe the main kinds of role in cybersecurity
Plan safe, legal ways to build experience
key_points: Security work spans many roles: analysts monitor and respond to alerts, engineers build and harden systems, governance and risk specialists set policy and check it's followed, and penetration testers are hired to test defences with permission.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 groups security work into six functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, a useful map of where each role fits.
The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NIST SP 800-181) describes security work roles and the knowledge and skills each needs.
Entry-level certifications, such as CompTIA Security+ and ISC2's Certified in Cybersecurity (CC), cover the fundamentals; check each one's current requirements and costs on its official website.

Build experience safely and legally on your own devices and virtual machines, with practice platforms and labs designed for learning; never test a system you don't own or have written permission to test.
Clear communication matters as much as technical skill: much of security work is explaining risks and choices to people who aren't specialists.

lab.title: Audit your home network
lab.goal: Review your own router's security settings, your Wi-Fi's security mode, the devices on your network and your computer's firewall, fix what you can, and record what you found.
setup: Your home router's admin password (sometimes on a label on the router)

steps.do: Find your router's address and your Wi-Fi's security mode with the commands from the lesson walkthrough, and record them.
Sign in to the router's admin page. If the admin password is still the one on the label, change it to a long unique one and save it in your password manager.
Find the firmware version (often under Administration, System or Maintenance) and install any update the router offers.
Check, and turn off unless you need them: remote management, WPS and UPnP. If you keep UPnP on, for example for a games console, note why.
Check the Wi-Fi security mode is WPA3 or WPA2 (AES), and turn on a guest network for visitors and smart devices if the router has one.
Open the list of connected devices. Identify each one, and note any you can't.
Check your computer's firewall is on, and turn it on if it isn't (on macOS: System Settings | Network | Firewall; on Ubuntu: sudo ufw enable).
steps.code:
netsh advfirewall show allprofiles state                 # Windows
/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate   # macOS
sudo ufw status                                         # Linux (Ubuntu)
steps.see: State ON for each profile on Windows, Firewall is enabled. (State = 1) on macOS, or Status: active on Ubuntu.

steps.do: Complete network-audit.md with what you found and every change you made.

checks.text: The router's admin password has been changed from the default and its firmware is up to date.
Remote management, WPS and UPnP have each been checked and set on purpose.
The Wi-Fi uses WPA2 (AES) or WPA3, shown by the computer's own report.
The computer's firewall is on, shown by the command's output.
Connected devices are identified, with a guest network used for visitors or smart devices where the router supports one.

lab.submit: Paste your completed network-audit.md, including the command output for the Wi-Fi security mode and the firewall. Leave out your Wi-Fi and admin passwords.

project.title: Write a security plan for a small office
project.brief: A six-person accounting practice has asked for a practical security plan. Each person has a laptop; there's a shared printer, a network storage box holding client files, cloud email and documents, a Wi-Fi router supplied by the internet provider, a smart TV in the waiting room and a card terminal at reception. Staff use their phones for email, a former employee left last month, and nobody is sure when the storage box was last backed up. Write a plan the practice's owner could follow, in plain language, using what you've learned: what to protect, the biggest risks, and the controls for accounts, devices, backups and the network, plus what to do when something goes wrong.
deliverables: An inventory of the practice's assets, each rated for confidentiality, integrity and availability
The five biggest risks, each with its likelihood, its impact and the controls that reduce it
An account policy: password manager, multi-factor authentication, administrator accounts, and joiners and leavers
A device and update policy, including encryption, screen locks and end-of-support devices
A 3-2-1 backup routine for the storage box and laptops, with a restore test schedule
A network plan: router settings, staff and guest networks, and where the TV and card terminal go
A one-page incident plan and a short staff guide to spotting and reporting phishing

rubric.name: Assets and risks
rubric.description: Assets are complete and sensibly rated for confidentiality, integrity and availability; the five risks are realistic for this office, with likelihood and impact explained.

rubric.name: Accounts and authentication
rubric.description: Unique passwords through a password manager, MFA everywhere it's offered (phishing-resistant where possible), separate admin accounts, and the former employee's access removed.

rubric.name: Devices, updates and backups
rubric.description: Automatic updates, encryption and screen locks on every device; end-of-support devices dealt with; a 3-2-1 routine with an offline or versioned copy and scheduled restore tests.

rubric.name: Network
rubric.description: Router hardened (admin password, firmware, WPS, remote management, UPnP), WPA2 or WPA3, and guests, the TV and the card terminal kept away from staff devices.

rubric.name: Incident plan and staff guidance
rubric.description: Clear first steps, contacts and how to restore; a phishing guide staff could actually use, including how and where to report.

rubric.name: Clarity
rubric.description: Plain language the owner could act on, with priorities ordered so the most important changes come first.
